import FormalConjecturesUtil

/-!
# Erdős Problem 387

*References:*
 - [erdosproblems.com/387](https://www.erdosproblems.com/387)
 - [ErGr76b] Erdős, P. and Graham, R. L., *On the prime factors of
   ${n \choose k}$*. Fibonacci Quart. (1976), 348-352.
 - [Er78g] Erdős, Pál, *On prime factors of binomial coefficients. II*. Mat. Lapok
   (1978/82), 307-316.
 - [ErGr80] Erdős, P. and Graham, R., *Old and new problems and results in combinatorial
   number theory*. Monographies de L'Enseignement Mathematique (1980).
 - [Sc58] Schinzel, A., *Sur un problème de P. Erdős*. Colloq. Math. (1958), 198-204.
 - [Gu04] Guy, Richard K., Unsolved problems in number theory. (2004), xviii+437.
 - [Fa66] Faulkner, M. "On a theorem of Sylvester and Schur." Journal of the London Mathematical
    Society 1.1 (1966): 107-110.
 - [BNPZ26] Bui, H., Naprienko, S., Pratt, K., and Zaharescu, A. Binomial coefficients with
    divisors avoiding an interval. arXiv:2605.21221 (2026).
-/

open Filter

namespace Erdos387

/--
Is there an absolute constant $c > 0$ such that, for all $1 \leq k < n$, the binomial coefficient
$\binom{n}{k}$ has a divisor in $(cn, n]$?

Bui, Naprienko, Pratt, and Zaharescu [BNPZ26] answered this negatively.
-/
@[category research solved, AMS 11]
theorem erdos_387 : answer(False) ↔ ∃ c : ℝ, 0 < c ∧ ∀ n k : ℕ, 1 ≤ k → k < n →
    ∃ d : ℕ, (d : ℝ) ∈ Set.Ioc (c * n) n ∧ d ∣ n.choose k := by
  sorry

@[category research solved, AMS 11]
example : ∀ i < 15, ¬ 99215 - i ∣ Nat.choose 99215 15 :=
  fun i hi => by interval_cases i <;> native_decide

/-- The following is Schinzel's conjecture, which appears in [Gu04]. -/
@[category research open, AMS 11]
theorem erdos_387.variants.schinzel : answer(sorry) ↔
    ∀ᶠ k in atTop, ¬ IsPrimePow k → ∃ n : ℕ, ∀ i < k, ¬ n - i ∣ n.choose k := by
  sorry

/-- It is easy to see that `n.choose k` has a divisor in `[n / k, n]`. -/
@[category research solved, AMS 11]
theorem erdos_387.variants.easy {n : ℕ} {k : ℕ} (hn : 1 ≤ n) (hk : k ≤ n) : ∃ d : ℕ,
    (d : ℝ) ∈ Set.Icc (n / k : ℝ) n ∧ d ∣ n.choose k := by
  by_cases k = 0 <;> simp_all
  refine ⟨(n.choose k).gcd n, ⟨?_, ?_⟩, gcd_dvd_left _ _⟩
  · rw [div_le_iff₀ (by positivity)]
    norm_cast
    rw [← Nat.gcd_mul_right]
    refine Nat.le_of_dvd ?_ (Nat.dvd_gcd ⟨(n - 1).choose (k - 1), ?_⟩ (dvd_mul_right _ _))
    · exact Nat.gcd_pos_of_pos_right _ (by positivity)
    · cases n <;> cases k <;> simp_all [Nat.add_one_mul_choose_eq]
  · exact Nat.le_of_dvd (by linarith) (gcd_dvd_right _ _)

/--
Is it true for any $c < 1$ and all $n$ sufficiently large, for all $1 \leq k < n$,
$\binom{n}{k}$ has a divisor in $(cn, n]$?

This variant appears in [Gu04]. Bui, Naprienko, Pratt, and Zaharescu [BNPZ26] answered it
negatively.
-/
@[category research solved, AMS 11]
theorem erdos_387.variants.guy : answer(False) ↔ ∀ c : ℝ, c < 1 → ∀ᶠ n : ℕ in atTop, ∀ k : ℕ, 1 ≤ k →
    k < n → ∃ d : ℕ, (d : ℝ) ∈ Set.Ioc (c * n) n ∧ d ∣ n.choose k := by
  sorry

end Erdos387

findings.description: The [Fa66] bibliography entry (lines 32–33) gives the journal volume/issue as “1.1”. Faulkner’s article is in the first series, volume 41, issue 1, not volume 1. This is a reference slip only; it does not affect any mathematical declaration.
findings.source_evidence: Wiley’s Crossref record for “On a Theorem of Sylvester and Schur”, DOI 10.1112/jlms/s1-41.1.107, specifies volume “s1-41”, issue “1”, pages 107–110, and publication year 1966: https://api.crossref.org/works/10.1112/jlms/s1-41.1.107.
findings.suggested_fix: Change the citation to “Journal of the London Mathematical Society, first series, 41(1) (1966), 107–110.”

reformulations.difference: Lean leaves the natural-number witness n unrestricted and excludes divisibility by n−i for every i<k, rather than explicitly imposing the nontrivial binomial range and excluding integer divisors in (n−k,n].
reformulations.equivalence_argument: For k>0, the nondivisibility condition itself forces k<n. If n<k, then n.choose k=0 and the condition fails already at i=0, since every natural number divides 0. If n=k, take i=k−1: the forbidden divisor is 1 and n.choose k=1. Once k<n, the numbers n−i for 0≤i<k are exactly the integers in (n−k,n]. Finally, eventual truth atTop on ℕ means truth for all k beyond some threshold, which can be enlarged to exclude k=0. The full equivalence with an explicit threshold, k<n, and interval nondivisibility was proved in the scratch file.

reformulations.difference: The theorem allows k=0 and k=n, extending the nontrivial range 1≤k<n used in the problem’s context. In particular, k=0 reaches Lean’s totalized real division.
reformulations.equivalence_argument: Both extra boundary cases hold independently with d=1. For k=0, n.choose 0=1 and the lower endpoint n/0 is 0; for k=n, n.choose n=1 and n/n=1 because n≥1. Thus the universally quantified statement is equivalent to its restriction to 1≤k<n. This equivalence was proved in Lean, so the zero-denominator case does not introduce a mathematical defect.

review.notes: No mathematical statement defects were found in the five assertions. The negative answers and solved tags for the main problem and Guy’s variant agree with BNPZ26 v2 and the problem page; Schinzel’s variant remains recorded as a conjecture. /workspace/review/scratch.lean compiles without errors and proves the reported equivalences without sorry. It also checks the small prime-power/binomial cases, all 15 nondivisibilities in the counterexample, and the gcd divisor bounds for 1≤k≤n≤50. Direct problem-page access was Cloudflare-blocked, so current mirrored text and the complete archived page were used. Gu04’s full text and Fa66’s full text were unavailable; Guy’s formulations are explicit on the cited problem page, and Fa66 appears only in the file’s bibliography. No repository files were changed.
